why: The longest continuous carbon chain is four carbons (butane) with a methyl branch. Numbering from the end nearest the branch places the methyl on C2, giving 2-methylbutane. 'Normal pentane' counts all five carbons as if they were in one straight chain, but the molecule is branched. '3-methylbutane' numbers from the wrong end (you must give the substituent the lowest locant). 'Isopentane' is the correct common name but not the IUPAC name. '2-methylpropane' undercounts the main chain by one carbon.

The strongest acid has the lowest pKa, which corresponds to the most stabilized conjugate base. Acetic acid (CH3COOH, pKa about 4.8) is strongest because its conjugate base, acetate, is resonance-stabilized over two equivalent oxygens. Ethanol and methanol (pKa about 16 and 15.5) form alkoxide bases with the charge on a single oxygen and no resonance delocalization. Methylamine (pKa about 40) and ethane (pKa about 50) are far weaker acids because their conjugate bases put the charge on less electronegative nitrogen or carbon.
note: water and ammonia replaced by methanol and methylamine so the key is not the longest formula; ranking unchanged
